# CANDIDATE 71 — the submission narrative

**17 Aug 2026. Generated by running G3 + G9 + G10 as a deliberate search rather than freelancing.**

> **The question the parts produced: what public, dated event commits someone to years of mandatory
> writing they do not want to do?**
>
> **The answer: every commercial insurance policy renews annually, and the broker must write a narrative
> to the underwriter each time.**

---

## 1. What was verified

**The narrative changes the price, and industry sources say so plainly:**

- *"Complete and **well-narrated** files get quoted first and priced with more confidence; **thin files sit
  in queues or draw conservative terms.**"*
- *"A strong narrative makes the underwriter's job easier — and underwriters who have an easy time with
  your submissions prioritize your work. **The underwriting narrative is often the difference between a
  fast review and multiple follow-ups.**"*
- What a strong narrative contains: *"risk controls: training routines, supervision, maintenance, quality
  checks, and how incidents are reported and investigated… changes in operations, new locations,
  outsourcing, contractual risk transfer, or any recent losses."*

**That is prose about a business, written to persuade a specific reader, on a hard deadline.** It is the
same engine as everything else on her board.

---

## 2. Parts firing — nine of them, and this is why it surfaced

| Part | How it applies |
|---|---|
| **G9 — the clock** | **Every commercial policy renews annually.** Not statutory, universal. Absolute recurrence with a hard date, and being late means the client goes to market late and gets worse terms |
| **G10 — expert buyer** | **The broker is the insurance expert.** She never claims to be. She is writing capacity |
| **G2 — Passport** | Qualify the **broker** once: their carriers, their classes of business, their format, their voice. Every renewal after that is a repeat |
| **G5 — invisible department** | *"You own the client. We're your invisible submission-narrative department"* |
| **G6 — corrected inversion** | The broker **has** the application, the loss runs, the prior submission and the client's own description — **and cannot turn it into persuasive prose in an afternoon when 200 renewals a year land on the desk.** Passes cleanly on the corrected test |
| **G12 — custody refusal as a feature** | **This is the competitive wedge.** Patra's entire model is working *inside* the client's AMS/DMS. *"We never touch your AMS"* is a differentiator, not an apology — and brokers who will not give offshore staff system access are precisely her market |
| **D6 — list source** | Insurance producers are licensed and **state licensing databases are public.** Enumerable, named, in writing |
| **D3 — partner recurrence** | One broker with 150 commercial accounts = **~12 renewals a month, forever** |
| **A4 — no stamp** | The broker signs and submits. She never advises on coverage |

**Economics, unverified but arithmetically simple:** at $200 a submission, one broker at 12/month is
**$2.400/month — her floor from a single relationship.** Commission on a mid-size commercial account runs
$2.000–20.000 a year, so a narrative that speeds a quote or improves terms is cheap at that price.

---

## 3. The occupancy check — and the distinction that matters

**Patra Corp is the incumbent, with 6.000+ process executives and 20M+ transactions a year.** Their own
description of what they do:

> *"certificate issuance, policy checking, claims services, endorsement processing, and **submission
> clearance**… they **gather documents within client AMS/DMS**, prepare submission(s) for market, complete
> surplus lines forms, and handle state website uploads and stamping."*

**That is document assembly, form completion and portal work — processing.** The persuasive narrative
describing the risk is a **different artefact**, and nothing in their material claims it.

> **Patra assembles the file. Nobody writes the story.**

**But the honest counterweight:** Patra works *inside the AMS*, which means the buyer's mental model of
"outsourcing" in this industry is *someone in my system.* Selling *"send me documents, I'll send you
prose"* is a different purchase that has to be explained. That is a marketing problem, not a structural
one — but it is real.

## 4. Where this is WORSE than candidate 70 — stated plainly

**This has better economics and worse constraint fit.** Both halves matter.

| | Candidate 70 (memorial → funeral homes) | Candidate 71 (narrative → brokers) |
|---|---|---|
| Money per unit | Lower | **Higher** |
| Frequency per partner | ~8 families/month | **~12 renewals/month** |
| Channel verified to buy outside vendors | **Yes** — Aftercare.com, Eterneva via Batesville | Unverified |
| Vendor already exists in the slot | **No** | Adjacent (Patra), not exact |
| **C1 — will they onboard in writing?** | Plausible — Aftercare.com sells at $150/mo *"no contracts"* | **Worse. Insurance is a phone industry.** Brokers do everything by call |
| Regulatory question | None | **Open — see below** |

> **The C1 risk is materially higher here than in funeral service, and C1 is her hardest constraint.**
> I am not going to bury that under the better arithmetic.

---

## 5. The open questions, in the order that decides it

1. **LICENSING — the one that could kill it outright.** Most states license anyone who *"solicits,
   negotiates, or sells"* insurance. Is preparing a submission narrative for a licensed broker back-office
   work, or does it touch the licensed perimeter? **She writes prose from documents the broker supplies;
   the broker reviews, signs and submits — which reads as back-office. UNVERIFIED, and this file has been
   killed by exactly this kind of question before** (PRUMO on CFC Res. 1.640/2021, Recurso on OAB Lei
   8.906/94).
2. **Will a broker buy from a written approach?** The C1 test at channel level, and insurance is the
   hardest environment yet for it.
3. **What do they pay?** No published price found for narrative writing specifically. Patra publishes no
   prices either.
4. **E&O.** If a narrative misstates a risk, the exposure sits with the broker who signed it — but the
   engagement wording needs to say so. **Observed condition, never a representation** (parts bin A4).
5. **The chatbot.** A broker can feed loss runs into a chatbot today. Same clock as every other candidate
   on this board.

---

## 6. What I would test first, free

**Not a pitch. A count.**

**Write one submission narrative from a real, public commercial risk** — a company with public filings,
public loss history and a describable operation — and send it, unsolicited and unpaid, to twenty licensed
commercial brokers found in state licensing databases, with one written question:

> *"Do you outsource submission narratives today, and if so to whom and at what price?"*

**Count the written answers containing a number.** That settles occupancy, price and the C1 channel
question simultaneously, costs nothing, and requires no phone.

**It is the same test shape agent 11 recommended for franchisors and agent 6 recommended for funeral
homes** — twenty real instances, count how many clear (**G17**).
